questions.q: What essential feature distinguishes a randomized experiment from an observational study?
choices: Treatments are actively imposed on experimental units by the researcher
A larger sample size is used
Participants are randomly surveyed by phone
Data is collected over a longer time period
questions.answer: In an experiment, researchers deliberately apply treatments to experimental units to observe responses. In observational studies, conditions are merely observed without intervention.

questions.q: Researchers observe that people who drink green tea daily have lower rates of cardiovascular disease. Can they conclude that green tea prevents heart disease?
choices: No, observational studies cannot establish cause-and-effect due to potential confounding variables
Yes, because the association is statistically significant
Yes, provided at least 10,000 subjects were observed
Only if green tea drinkers were matched by age
questions.answer: Causation cannot be inferred from observational studies because lifestyle, diet, or exercise factors may confound the relationship.

questions.q: Only which type of statistical investigation allows researchers to establish cause-and-effect conclusions?
choices: A well-designed randomized comparative experiment
A large-scale stratified observational study
A voluntary response poll with $n > 50,000$
A census of the population
questions.answer: Only well-controlled experiments with random assignment of treatments can establish causal relationships.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of random assignment in an experiment?
choices: To create roughly equivalent treatment groups and balance out confounding variables
To ensure the sample represents the entire population
To eliminate all experimental error
To prevent the need for a control group
questions.answer: Random assignment balances the effects of uncontrolled extraneous variables across treatment groups, ensuring differences in response can be attributed to the treatments.

questions.q: What role does a control group serve in an experiment?
choices: Provides a baseline measurement to compare against active treatments
Ensures the experiment has a large enough sample size
Guarantees that subjects do not know which treatment they receive
Eliminates the need for replication
questions.answer: A control group serves as a baseline comparison to evaluate whether changes in the response variable are truly due to the active treatment.

questions.q: In experimental design, what does 'replication' mean?
choices: Assigning multiple experimental units to each treatment group
Repeating the entire experiment in another country
Using identical equipment across all trials
Testing subjects multiple times in a row
questions.answer: Replication means applying treatments to sufficiently many experimental units so that treatment effects can be distinguished from chance variation.

choices: Neither the subjects nor the individuals evaluating the outcomes know which treatment each subject received
Neither the researcher nor the subjects know the purpose of the study
The experiment is conducted in a darkened laboratory
Both the control group and treatment group receive identical active medications
questions.answer: In a double-blind study, neither the participants nor the evaluators/data recorders know which treatment was assigned, preventing psychological and diagnostic bias.

choices: When subjects show improvement simply from the psychological expectation of receiving a treatment
When a drug causes adverse side effects in control patients
When experimental units drop out of a clinical trial
When researchers unconsciously bias results
questions.answer: The placebo effect occurs when patients respond positively to an inactive treatment due to the psychological expectation of healing.

choices: A variable related to both the explanatory variable and response variable that obscures whether the treatment caused the outcome
A variable that is held constant across all treatment conditions
A calculation error during hypothesis testing
A categorical variable with more than two levels
questions.answer: A confounding variable is associated with the treatment group assignment and also affects the response, making it impossible to isolate the treatment's effect.

sections.heading: Section 4: Blocking and Scope of Inference

questions.q: When should an experimenter implement a randomized block design?
choices: When there is an identified characteristic expected to affect the response, so subjects are grouped by that trait before randomization
When the sample size is too small for simple random assignment
When double-blinding is completely impossible
To avoid having to use a control group
questions.answer: Blocking groups units by a known source of variability (e.g. age, gender) prior to random assignment of treatments, reducing unexplained variation within blocks.

questions.q: A matched pairs design is a special form of:
choices: Block design
Cluster sampling
Stratified survey
Completely randomized design
questions.answer: Matched pairs is a block design where blocks consist of pairs of closely matched units, or where each subject receives both treatments in random order.

questions.q: If subjects are volunteers (not randomly selected from a population) but are randomly assigned to treatments, what inference can be drawn?
choices: Causation can be inferred, but only for individuals similar to the volunteer participants
Results can be generalized to the entire national population
No valid statistical conclusions can be drawn
Association only, causation cannot be established
questions.answer: Random assignment allows causal inference; lack of random selection from the population limits generalizability to subjects similar to those who participated.
